'''David Lee Chaum''' (born 1955) is an American [[computer scientist]], [[List of cryptographers|cryptographer]], and inventor. He is known as a pioneer in cryptography and privacy-preserving technologies and widely recognized as the inventor of [[Digital currency|digital cash]]. His 1982 dissertation, "Computer Systems Established, Maintained, and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups," is the first known proposal for a [[blockchain]] protocol.<ref name="Sherman et al.">{{cite journal |author=Alan T. Sherman, Farid Javani, Haibin Zhang, Enis Golaszewski |title=On the Origins and Variations of Blockchain Technologies |journal=IEEE Security & Privacy |date=January–February 2019 |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=72–77 |doi=10.1109/MSEC.2019.2893730|arxiv=1810.06130 |bibcode=2019ISPri..17a..72S |s2cid=53114747 }}</ref> Complete with the code to implement the protocol, Chaum's dissertation proposed all but one element of the blockchain later detailed in the [[Bitcoin]] [[White paper|whitepaper]]. He has been referred to as "the father of online anonymity",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/2016/01/david-chaum-father-of-online-anonymity-plan-to-end-the-crypto-wars/|title=The Father of Online Anonymity Has a Plan to End the Crypto War|first1=Andy|last1=Greenberg|publisher=Wired Magazine|date=January 6, 2016|access-date=February 8, 2022|archive-date=May 7, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230507072730/https://www.wired.com/2016/01/david-chaum-father-of-online-anonymity-plan-to-end-the-crypto-wars/|url-status=live}}</ref> and "the godfather of cryptocurrency."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-05-27/meet-the-godfather-of-crypto-who-s-been-working-on-digital-currency-since-the-early-80s|title=Meet The Godfather Of Crypto, Who's Been Working On Digital Currency Since The Early 80s|publisher=Bloomberg News|date=May 27, 2019|access-date=2022-03-05|archive-date=2022-03-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305044834/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-05-27/meet-the-godfather-of-crypto-who-s-been-working-on-digital-currency-since-the-early-80s|url-status=live}}</ref>

He is also known for developing [[ecash]], an electronic cash application that aims to preserve a user's anonymity, and inventing many [[cryptography|cryptographic]] protocols like the [[blind signature]], [[mix networks]], and the [[Dining cryptographers protocol|Dining Cryptographers Protocol]]. In 1995, his company [[DigiCash]] created the first digital currency with eCash.<ref name="Greenberg">Greenberg, Andy (2012). ''This Machine Kills Secrets: How WikiLeakers, Cypherpunks, and Hacktivists Aim to Free the World's Information.'' Dutton Adult.  {{ISBN|0525953205}}.</ref>{{rp|65–70}} His 1981 paper, "Untraceable Electronic Mail, Return Addresses, and Digital Pseudonyms," laid the groundwork for the field of anonymous communications research.<ref>Danezis, George; Diaz, Claudia (January 2008) "[https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-survey-of-anonymous-communication-channels/ Survey of Anonymous Communication Channels] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519194543/https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-survey-of-anonymous-communication-channels/ |date=2023-05-19 }}" [https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2008/02/tr-2008-35.pdf PDF] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519194612/https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2008/02/tr-2008-35.pdf |date=2023-05-19 }}. Technical Report MSR-TR-2008-35. Microsoft Research; For the paper, see {{cite journal | last1 = Chaum | first1 = David | year = 1981 | title = Untraceable Electronic Mail, Return Addresses, and Digital Pseudonyms | url = http://www.cs.utexas.edu/~shmat/courses/cs395t_fall04/chaum81.pdf | journal = Communications of the ACM | volume = 24 | issue = 2 | pages = 84–90 | doi = 10.1145/358549.358563 | s2cid = 30340230 | access-date = 2019-09-24 | archive-date = 2020-09-19 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200919013417/http://www.cs.utexas.edu/~shmat/courses/cs395t_fall04/chaum81.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref>

More recently, in 2020, Chaum founded the [[xx network]], a privacy-focused blockchain platform, and in 2021 launched [[xx network|xx coin]] (abbreviation XX), a cryptocurrency designed to enhance user privacy and provide quantum resistance.<ref>https://xxfoundation.org/directory/ | https://xx.network/blog/xxcoin-tokenomics/</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.crowdfundinsider.com/2019/11/154425-digital-currency-pioneer-david-chaum-announces-upcoming-release-of-xx-network-a-blockchain-for-conducting-secure-transctions/ | title=Digital Currency Pioneer David Chaum Announces Upcoming Release of Xx Network, A Blockchain for Conducting Secure Transctions &#124; Crowdfund Insider | date=24 November 2019 }}</ref>

== Life and career ==

Chaum was born to a [[Jews|Jewish]] family in [[Los Angeles, California]].<ref name="Levy">Levy, Steven (2012). ''Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government--Saving Privacy in the Digital Age''. Penguin Books.  {{ISBN|9781101199466}}.</ref> He gained a doctorate in computer science from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1982.<ref name=":0">David Lee Chaum. [https://books.google.com/books?id=bbeNnAEACAAJ "Computer Systems Established, Maintained and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups." University of California, Berkeley, 1982.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510181055/https://books.google.com/books?id=bbeNnAEACAAJ |date=2023-05-10 }}</ref><ref name="Pitta">Pitta, Julie (November 1, 1999). "{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20050415140654/http://www.forbes.com/forbes/1999/1101/6411390a_print.html Requiem for a Bright Idea]}}". ''Forbes''.</ref> Also that year, he founded the [[International Association for Cryptologic Research]] (IACR), which currently organizes academic conferences in cryptography research.<ref name="Blanchette">Blanchette, Jean-François (2012). ''Burdens of Proof: Cryptographic Culture and Evidence Law in the Age of Electronic Documents''. MIT Press. {{ISBN|026230080X}}.</ref>{{rp|47}} Subsequently, he taught at the [[New York University]] Graduate School of Business Administration and at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] (UCSB). He also formed a cryptography research group at [[Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica|CWI]], the Dutch National Research Institute for Mathematics and Computer Science in [[Amsterdam]].<ref name="idtrail1">{{cite web |url=http://www.idtrail.org/content/view/28/ |title=On the Identity Trail - David Chaum: Bio |access-date=2013-06-13 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202223014/http://www.idtrail.org/content/view/28/ |archive-date=2013-12-02 }}</ref> He founded [[DigiCash]], an electronic cash company, in 1990.<ref name="Greenberg"/>{{rp|119}}

Chaum received the Information Technology European Award for 1995.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rotenberg|first=Marc|title=Eurocrats Do Good Privacy|url=https://www.wired.com/wired/archive/4.05/eurocrats_pr.html|access-date=June 17, 2013|newspaper=Wired Magazine|date=May 1, 1996|archive-date=March 28, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140328175512/http://www.wired.com/wired/archive/4.05/eurocrats_pr.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2004, he was named an IACR Fellow.<ref>{{cite web|title=IACR Fellows|url=https://www.iacr.org/fellows/|publisher=IACR|access-date=June 17, 2013|archive-date=April 24, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180424213547/https://www.iacr.org/fellows/|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2010, at the [[RSA Conference]], he was honored with the [[RSA Award for Excellence in Mathematics]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://365.rsaconference.com/community/__archived_content/rsa-conference-usa-2010/blog/2010/03/02/congratulations-to-this-year-s-rsa-conference-2010-award-winners |title=RSA Conference &#124; RSA Conference USA 2010 &#124; Congratulations to this year's RSA Conference 2010 Award winners! |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130616032659/https://365.rsaconference.com/community/__archived_content/rsa-conference-usa-2010/blog/2010/03/02/congratulations-to-this-year-s-rsa-conference-2010-award-winners |archive-date=2013-06-16 }}</ref> In 2019, he was awarded the honorary title of Dijkstra Fellow by CWI.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cwi.nl/news/2019/david-chaum-and-guido-van-rossum-awarded-dijkstra-fellowship|title=David Chaum and Guido van Rossum awarded Dijkstra Fellowship|website=CWI|access-date=2019-11-22|archive-date=2022-12-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207123113/https://www.cwi.nl/news/2019/david-chaum-and-guido-van-rossum-awarded-dijkstra-fellowship|url-status=live}}</ref> He received an honorary doctorate from the [[Università della Svizzera Italiana|University of Lugano]] in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usi.ch/en/university/who-we-are/honorary-doctorate |title=USI Honorary Doctorates |publisher=USI |access-date=May 16, 2021 |archive-date=June 3, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603182920/https://www.usi.ch/en/university/who-we-are/honorary-doctorate |url-status=live }}</ref>

Chaum resides in [[Sherman Oaks, Los Angeles]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/e-cash-inventor-david-chaum-201555305.html|title=E-cash inventor David Chaum on making a comeback, pre-empting bitcoin, and keeping Satoshi anonymous|website=finance.yahoo.com|date=23 April 2019|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-02|archive-date=2022-06-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220610153835/https://finance.yahoo.com/news/e-cash-inventor-david-chaum-201555305.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Notable research contributions ==

=== Vault systems ===
Recently credited by [[Alan Sherman]]'s "On the Origins and Variations of Blockchain Technologies",<ref name="Sherman et al."/> Chaum's 1982 Berkeley dissertation proposed every element of the [[blockchain]] found in [[Bitcoin]] except [[proof of work]]. The proposed vault system lays out a plan for achieving consensus state between nodes, chaining the history of consensus in blocks, and immutably time-stamping the chained data. The paper also lays out the specific code to implement such a protocol.

=== Digital cash ===

Chaum is credited as the inventor of secure digital cash for his 1983 paper, which also introduced the cryptographic primitive of a [[blind signature]].<ref name="Cha82">{{cite book |first=David |last=Chaum |title=Advances in Cryptology |chapter=Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments |year=1983 |volume=82 |issue=3 |pages=199–203 |publisher=Springer |location=Boston, MA |chapter-url=http://www.hit.bme.hu/~buttyan/courses/BMEVIHIM219/2009/Chaum.BlindSigForPayment.1982.PDF |doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-0602-4_18 |isbn=978-1-4757-0604-8 |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-date=2014-12-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218034712/http://www.hit.bme.hu/%7Ebuttyan/courses/BMEVIHIM219/2009/Chaum.BlindSigForPayment.1982.PDF |url-status=live }}</ref> These ideas have been described as the technical roots of the vision of the [[Cypherpunk]] movement that began in the late 1980s.<ref name="narayanan">Arvind Narayanan: [http://randomwalker.info/publications/crypto-dream-part1.pdf What Happened to the Crypto Dream?, Part 1] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029143759/http://randomwalker.info/publications/crypto-dream-part1.pdf |date=2019-10-29 }}.  ''IEEE Security & Privacy''. Volume 11, Issue 2, March–April 2013, pages 75-76, ISSN 1540-7993</ref> Chaum's proposal allowed users to obtain digital currency from a bank and spend it in a manner that is untraceable by the bank or any other party.<ref name="Cha85">{{cite journal | first = David | last = Chaum | author-link = David Chaum | title = Security without identification: transaction systems to make big brother obsolete | journal = Communications of the ACM | volume = 28 | date=October 1985 | issue = 10 | doi = 10.1145/4372.4373 | pages = 1030–1044 | s2cid = 15340054 | url = https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/4372.4373 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20240419092956/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/4372.4373 | archive-date = 2024-04-19 | access-date = 2024-08-21 }}</ref>
In 1988, he extended this idea (with [[Amos Fiat]] and [[Moni Naor]]) to allow offline transactions that enable detection of double-spending.<ref name="CFN88">{{citation
 | last1 = Chaum | first1 = D.
 | last2 = Fiat | first2 = A.
 | last3 = Naor | first3 = M.
 | contribution = Untraceable electronic cash
 | location = London, UK
 | pages = 319–327
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Proceedings on Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO '88
 | volume = 403
 | year = 1990}}</ref>

In 1990, he founded [[DigiCash]], an electronic cash company, in Amsterdam to commercialize the ideas in his research.<ref name="Greenberg"/>{{rp|119}} The first electronic payment was sent in 1994.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://w2.eff.org/Privacy/Digital_money/?f=digicash.announce.txt |title=EFF: |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150107040853/https://w2.eff.org/Privacy/Digital_money/?f=digicash.announce.txt |archive-date=2015-01-07 }}</ref> In 1998, DigiCash filed for bankruptcy, and in 1999 Chaum sold off DigiCash and ended his involvement with the company.<ref name="idtrail1"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Pitta |first1=Julie |title=Requiem for a Bright Idea |url=https://www.forbes.com/forbes/1999/1101/6411390a.html |access-date=8 October 2022 |work=Forbes |date=1 November 1999 |language=en |archive-date=30 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830214226/https://www.forbes.com/forbes/1999/1101/6411390a.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Awards ===
In 2021, Chaum, [[Claude Crépeau|Claude Crépeau,]] and [[Ivan Damgård]] received a [https://sigact.org/prizes/stoc_tot.html 30-Year STOC Test of Time Award] from the [https://www.acm.org/special-interest-groups/sigs/sigact ACM Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computation Theory (SIGACT)] for their 1988 paper,  [https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/62212.62214 "Multiparty Unconditionally Secure Protocols."]  The paper was recognized as one of three seminal works on information-theoretically secure multiparty computation. [https://chaum.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/sigact-org-prizes-stoc-tot.pdf]

=== New types of digital signatures ===

In the same 1982 paper that proposed digital cash, Chaum introduced [[blind signature]]s.<ref name="Cha82"/> This form of [[digital signature]] blinds the content of a message before it is signed, so that the signer cannot determine the content. The resulting blind signature can be publicly verified against the original, unblinded message in the manner of a regular digital signature.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2339 |title=RSA Laboratories - 7.3 What is a blind signature scheme? |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120826003324/http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2339 |archive-date=2012-08-26 }}</ref>

In 1989, he (with Hans van Antwerpen) introduced [[undeniable signature]]s.<ref name="CV89">{{cite book|last1=Chaum|first1=David|last2=van Antwerpen|first2=Hans |title=Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO' 89 Proceedings |chapter=Undeniable Signatures |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=1990|volume=435|pages=212–216 |doi=10.1007/0-387-34805-0_20|isbn=978-0-387-97317-3 }}</ref> This form of digital signature uses a verification process that is interactive, so that the signatory can limit who can verify the signature. Since signers may refuse to participate in the verification process, signatures are considered valid unless a signer specifically uses a disavowal protocol to prove that a given signature was not authentic.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2344 |title=RSA Laboratories - 7.8 What is an undeniable signature scheme? |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120820015410/http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2344 |archive-date=2012-08-20 }}</ref>

In 1991, he (with Eugene van Heyst) introduced [[group signature]]s, which allow a member of a group to anonymously sign a message on behalf of the entire group.<ref name="CH91">{{cite book | first1 = David | last1 = Chaum | first2 = Eugene | last2 = van Heyst | title = Advances in Cryptology – EUROCRYPT '91 | chapter = Group Signatures | volume = 547 | series = [[Lecture Notes in Computer Science]] | year = 1991 | pages = 257–265 | chapter-url = https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/3-540-46416-6_22.pdf | doi = 10.1007/3-540-46416-6_22 | isbn = 978-3-540-54620-7 | doi-access = free | access-date = 2023-05-13 | archive-date = 2023-05-13 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230513074428/https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/3-540-46416-6_22.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref> However an appointed group manager holds the power to revoke the anonymity of any signer in the case of disputes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2342 |title=RSA Laboratories - 7.6 What is a group signature? |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120820015447/http://www.rsa.com/rsalabs/node.asp?id=2342 |archive-date=2012-08-20 }}</ref>

=== Anonymous communication ===

In 1981, Chaum proposed the idea of an anonymous communication network in a paper.<ref name="Cha81">{{Cite journal | last1 = Chaum | first1 = D. L. | title = Untraceable electronic mail, return addresses, and digital pseudonyms | doi = 10.1145/358549.358563 | journal = Communications of the ACM | volume = 24 | issue = 2 | pages = 84–90 | year = 1981 | s2cid = 30340230 | url = https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/358549.358563 | access-date = 2019-09-24 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200919013417/http://www.cs.utexas.edu/~shmat/courses/cs395t_fall04/chaum81.pdf | archive-date = 2020-09-19 | url-status = live }}</ref>
His proposal, called [[mix network]]s, allows a group of senders to submit an encryption of a message and its recipient to a server. Once the server has a batch of messages, it will reorder and obfuscate the messages so that only this server knows which message came from which sender. The batch is then forwarded to another server who does the same process. Eventually, the messages reach the final server where they are fully decrypted and delivered to the recipient. A mechanism to allow return messages is also proposed. Mix networks are the basis of some [[Anonymous remailer|remailers]] and are the conceptual ancestor to modern anonymous web browsing tools like [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor]] (based on [[onion routing]]). Chaum has advocated that every router be made, effectively, a Tor node.<ref>{{YouTube|id=WqgHh7KXTFM#t=44m55s}}</ref>

In 1988, Chaum introduced a different type of anonymous communication system called a DC-Net, which is a solution to his proposed [[Dining cryptographers problem|Dining Cryptographers Problem]].<ref name="Cha88">{{cite journal | author=David Chaum | title=The Dining Cryptographers Problem: Unconditional Sender and Recipient Untraceability | journal=Journal of Cryptology | volume=1 | issue=1 | year=1988 | pages=65–75 | doi=10.1007/BF00206326 | url=https://www.cs.cornell.edu/People/egs/herbivore/dcnets.html | s2cid=2664614 | access-date=2013-06-13 | archive-date=2014-12-21 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221230944/http://www.cs.cornell.edu/People/egs/herbivore/dcnets.html | url-status=live }}</ref> DC-Nets is the basis of the software tool Dissent.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://korz.cs.yale.edu/2010/anon/ |title=Dedis@yale &#124; Dissent: Accountable Anonymous Group Communication |access-date=2013-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130828211635/http://korz.cs.yale.edu/2010/anon/ |archive-date=2013-08-28 }}</ref>

In 2017, Chaum published a description of a new variety of mix network.<ref>Chaum, D., Das, D., Javani, F., Kate, A., Krasnova, A., Ruiter, J.D., & Sherman, A.T. (2017). cMix: Mixing with Minimal Real-Time Asymmetric Cryptographic Operations. ''ACNS''.</ref> A real-world implementation of this network, called cMix and running on the [[xx network]], later became the [[Data transmission protocol|data transmission layer]] for the [[instant messaging]] platform [[xx messenger]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Greenberg |first=Andy |title=The Father of Online Anonymity Has a Plan to End the Crypto War |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2016/01/david-chaum-father-of-online-anonymity-plan-to-end-the-crypto-wars/ |access-date=2022-09-02 |issn=1059-1028 |archive-date=2023-05-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230507072730/https://www.wired.com/2016/01/david-chaum-father-of-online-anonymity-plan-to-end-the-crypto-wars/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Trustworthy voting systems ===

Chaum has made numerous contributions to secure voting systems, including the first proposal of a system that is [[End-to-end auditable voting systems|end-to-end verifiable]]. This proposal, made in 1981,<ref name="Cha81"/> was given as an application of mix networks. In this system, the individual ballots of voters were kept private which anyone could verify that the tally was counted correctly. This, and other early cryptographic voting systems, assumed that voters could reliably compute values with their personal computers. In 1991,{{Citation needed|date=April 2021|reason=Cited paper is 2001, not 1991}} Chaum introduced SureVote which allowed voters to cast a ballot from an untrustworthy voting system,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Chaum|first=David|date=2001|title=SureVote: Technical Overview. Proceedings of the Workshop on Trustworthy Elections (WOTE '01).|url=https://www.vote.caltech.edu/wote01/pdfs/surevote.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081023130048/https://www.vote.caltech.edu/wote01/pdfs/surevote.pdf|archive-date=2008-10-23}}</ref> proposing a process now called "code voting" and used in remote voting systems like Remotegrity and DEMOS.<ref>Filip Zagorski and Richard T. Carback and David Chaum and Jeremy Clark and Aleksander Essex and Poorvi L. Vora (2013), "[http://eprint.iacr.org/2013/214 Remotegrity: Design and Use of an End-to-End Verifiable Remote Voting System] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624174026/http://eprint.iacr.org/2013/214 |date=2013-06-24 }}," ''11th International Conference on Applied Cryptography and Network Security (ACNS 2013)''.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=E2E-VIV Project {{!}} U.S. Vote Foundation|url=https://www.usvotefoundation.org/E2E-VIV|access-date=2021-04-28|website=www.usvotefoundation.org|archive-date=2016-09-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160911100823/https://www.usvotefoundation.org/E2E-VIV|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1994, Chaum introduced the first in-person voting system in which voters cast ballots electronically at a polling station and cryptographically verify that the DRE did not modify their vote (or even learn what it was).<ref>Declan McCullagh, [https://www.cnet.com/tech/tech-industry/high-hopes-for-unscrambling-the-vote/ "High hopes for unscrambling the vote"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519163638/https://www.cnet.com/tech/tech-industry/high-hopes-for-unscrambling-the-vote/ |date=2023-05-19 }}, CNET News, October 1, 2004.</ref> In the following years, Chaum proposed (often with others) a series a cryptographically verifiable voting systems that use conventional paper ballots: [[Prêt à Voter]],<ref>
{{Citation
 |first=D. 
 |last=Chaum 
 |author2=P.Y.A. Ryan 
 |author3=S. Schneider 
 |chapter=A Practical Voter-Verifiable Election Scheme 
 |chapter-url=http://www.pretavoter.com/publications/esorics05.pdf 
 |title=Computer Security – ESORICS 2005
 |volume=3679 
 |pages=118–139 
 |year=2005 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314094556/http://www.pretavoter.com/publications/esorics05.pdf 
 |archive-date=2012-03-14 
 |doi=10.1007/11555827_8 
 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science 
 |isbn=978-3-540-28963-0 
 }}</ref> [[Punchscan]],<ref>S. Cherry, [https://spectrum.ieee.org/making-every-evote-count "Making Every E-Vote Count"], ''IEEE Spectrum'', Jan 1 2007.</ref> and [[Scantegrity]].<ref>M. Lafsky, [http://discovermagazine.com/2008/oct/04-protecting-your-vote-with-invisible-ink#.UbxhzRZZWxI "Protecting Your Vote With Invisible Ink,"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131101173501/http://discovermagazine.com/2008/oct/04-protecting-your-vote-with-invisible-ink#.UbxhzRZZWxI |date=2013-11-01 }} Discover Magazine, Oct 2008.</ref> The city of [[Takoma Park, Maryland]] used Scantegrity for its November, 2009 election.<ref>{{Citation
 |title       = Pilot Study of the Scantegrity II Voting System Planned for the 2009 Takoma Park City Election
 |url         = http://www.takomaparkmd.gov/committees/boe/documents/flyer_workshop_I_(02-19-09).pdf
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719064407/http://www.takomaparkmd.gov/committees/boe/documents/flyer_workshop_I_%2802-19-09%29.pdf
 |archive-date = July 19, 2011
}}</ref> This was the first time a public sector election was run using any cryptographically verifiable voting system.<ref>{{Citation
| last = Hardesty
| first = Larry
| title = Cryptographic voting debuts
| work = MIT news
| date = 2009-11-13
| access-date = 2023-05-19
| url = https://news.mit.edu/2009/rivest-voting
| archive-date = 2023-05-19
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230519165140/https://news.mit.edu/2009/rivest-voting
| url-status = live
}}</ref>

In 2011, Chaum proposed Random Sample Elections.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rs-elections.com/|title=Random Sample Elections|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130623004543/http://rs-elections.com/|archive-date=2013-06-23|access-date=2013-06-28}}</ref> This electoral system allows a verifiably random selection of voters, who can maintain their anonymity, to cast votes on behalf the entire electorate.<ref>Joshua Davis. "[https://www.wired.com/2012/05/st-essay-voting/ How Selecting Voters Randomly Can Lead to Better Elections] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230106191157/https://www.wired.com/2012/05/st-essay-voting/ |date=2023-01-06 }}." Wired, 16.05.2012.</ref>

=== Other contributions ===

In a 1979 report published as Memorandum No. UCB/ERL M79/10<ref>{{Cite report | last = Chaum | first = David L. | title = Computer Systems Established, Maintained, and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups | date = February 22, 1979 | url = https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/1979/ERL-m-79-10.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220615040203/https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/1979/ERL-m-79-10.pdf | archive-date = 2022-06-15 | publisher = University of California, Berkeley, Electronics Research Laboratory | series = Memorandum | number = UCB/ERL M79/10 | access-date = 2024-08-21 }}</ref> by the Electronics Research Laboratory at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], Chaum proposed a mechanism for splitting a cryptographic key into partial keys that could be distributed among mutually suspicious groups. This concept was a significant predecessor to what is now known as [[secret sharing]].<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Chaum | first1 = D. | title = Advances in Cryptology | chapter = How to Keep a Secret Alive | doi = 10.1007/3-540-39568-7_40 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume = 196 | pages = 481–485 | year = 1985 | publisher = Springer | location = Berlin, Heidelberg | isbn = 978-3-540-15658-1 | chapter-url = https://chaum.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Chaum1985-Chapter-How-To-Keep-a-Secret-Alive.pdf | access-date = 2024-08-21 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230316080459/https://chaum.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Chaum1985-Chapter-How-To-Keep-a-Secret-Alive.pdf | archive-date = 2023-03-16 | url-status = live }}</ref>

In 1985, Chaum proposed the original [[Digital credential|anonymous credential]] system,<ref name="Cha85"/> which is sometimes also referred to as a pseudonym system.<ref>{{cite book | first1 = Anna | last1 = Lysyanskaya|author1-link=Anna Lysyanskaya | author-link2 = Ron Rivest | first2 = Ronald L. | last2 = Rivest | first3 = Amit | last3 = Sahai | first4 = Stefan | last4 = Wolf | chapter = Pseudonym systems | title = Selected Areas in Cryptography | editor1-link = Howard Heys | editor1-first = Howard M. | editor1-last = Heys | editor2-link = Carlisle Adams | editor2-first = Carlisle M. | editor2-last = Adams | series = [[Lecture Notes in Computer Science]] | volume = 1758 | publisher = Springer | year = 2000 | isbn = 978-3-540-67185-5 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-46513-8_14 | pages = 184–199| title-link = Selected Areas in Cryptography| s2cid = 77189}}</ref> This stems from the fact that the credentials of such a system are obtained from and shown to organizations using different pseudonyms that cannot be linked.

In 1988, Chaum with [[Gilles Brassard]] and [[Claude Crépeau]] published a paper <ref name="BCC88">Gilles Brassard, David Chaum, and Claude Crepeau, ''[http://crypto.cs.mcgill.ca/~crepeau/PDF/BCC88-jcss.pdf Minimum Disclosure Proofs of Knowledge] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927181436/http://crypto.cs.mcgill.ca/~crepeau/PDF/BCC88-jcss.pdf |date=2011-09-27 }}'', Journal of Computer and System Sciences, vol. 37, pp. 156–189, 1988. </ref> that introduced [[Zero-knowledge proofs|zero-knowledge arguments]], as well as a security model using information-theoretic private channels, and also first formalized the concept of a [[commitment scheme]].

1991, with Torben Pedersen, he demonstrated a well-cited [[zero-knowledge proof]] of a [[Decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption|DDH tuple]].<ref name="CP92">David Chaum and Torben P. Pedersen. 1992. Wallet Databases with Observers. In Proceedings of the 12th Annual International Cryptology Conference on Advances in Cryptology (CRYPTO '92), Ernest F. Brickell (Ed.). Springer-Verlag, London, UK, UK, 89-105.</ref> This proof is particularly useful as it can prove proper reencryption of an [[ElGamal encryption|ElGamal]] ciphertext.

Chaum contributed to an important [[commitment scheme]] which is often attributed to Pedersen. In fact, Pedersen, in his 1991 paper,<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Pedersen | first1 = T. P. | chapter = Non-Interactive and Information-Theoretic Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing | doi = 10.1007/3-540-46766-1_9 | title = Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO '91 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume = 576 | pages = 129–140 | year = 1992 | publisher = Springer | location = Berlin, Heidelberg | isbn = 978-3-540-55188-1 }}</ref> cites a rump session talk on an unpublished paper by Jurjen Bos and Chaum for the scheme. It appeared even earlier in a paper by Chaum, Damgard, and Jeroen van de Graaf.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Chaum | first1 = D. | last2 = Damgård | first2 = I. B. | last3 = Graaf | first3 = J. | doi = 10.1007/3-540-48184-2_7 | chapter = Multiparty Computations Ensuring Privacy of Each Party's Input and Correctness of the Result | title = Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO '87 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume = 293 | page = 87 | year = 1988 | isbn = 978-3-540-18796-7 }}</ref>

In 1993 with [[Stefan Brands]], Chaum introduced the concept of a [[distance-bounding protocol]].<ref name="BC93">Stefan Brands, David Chaum: Distance-bounding protocols (extended abstract). Proceedings of Eurocrypt '93.</ref>

In 2019, he was one of the speakers at the fifth [[Ethereum]] developer conference, which was held in [[Japan]].<ref>{{YouTube|hvdxT_uO0dc|David Chaum (Devcon5)}}</ref>

In July 2024, Chaum was on a panel on the future of privacy at the Plasmacon conference at the [[United Nations University]] in Tokyo, Japan, with [[Vitalik Buterin]], co-founder of [[Ethereum]].<ref>{{YouTube|hLpGXchvaMM|David Chaum & Vitalik Buterin - Plasmacon - Future of Privacy}}</ref>
